--- title: "[Graph.line_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Return the line graph of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L19915-L20064){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.line_graph(create_using_directed=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Line graph](/assets/graphs/line-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A four-node graph whose edges AB, BC, CD and BD each have their own color. In the line graph each of those edges becomes a node of the same color, named after it, and two nodes are joined when their edges share an endpoint; AB and CD share none, so they stay unconnected." width="100%"} The line graph `L(G)` of a graph `G` transforms edges into nodes: each edge in `G` becomes a node in `L(G)`, and two nodes in `L(G)` are connected if and only if their corresponding edges in `G` share an endpoint. Turning edges into nodes lets you apply any node-level tool to edges. Common uses: - finding edge communities (overlapping communities of nodes) by running a community detection method on the line graph - computing centrality of edges, e.g., which road segments or links are most central - modeling transfers in transport networks, where moving from one route segment to the next happens at a shared stop - edge coloring problems, which become node coloring problems on `L(G)` For an undirected graph, every pair of edges meeting at a node is connected, so a node of degree `d` contributes `d * (d - 1) / 2` edges to the line graph. Line graphs of graphs with hubs can therefore be much larger than the original. For a directed graph, edge `(u, v)` is linked to edge `(v, w)` only when the first edge ends where the second begins, which follows paths through the network. Each line-graph node is labelled `"-"` using the original node *IDs* (e.g., `"1-2"`). If the graph has parallel edges between the same pair of nodes, the original edge ID is appended (e.g., `"1-2-e3"`) to keep labels unique. Original node attributes are not carried over, and line-graph edges have no weights or attributes. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [create_using_directed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether the resulting line graph should be marked as directed. - If `None` (default): inherits directedness from source graph - If `True`: creates a directed line graph - If `False`: creates an undirected line graph This only sets the directedness of the returned graph; which pairs of edges are connected is always decided by the directedness of the *source* graph. For a directed source, edge `(u,v)` connects to edge `(v,w)` if they share the intermediate node `v` (i.e., head of first = tail of second); with `create_using_directed=False` those same connections are kept but without direction. For an undirected source with `create_using_directed=True`, each connection becomes a single directed edge from the lower to the higher line-graph node ID, not a pair. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new Graph representing the line graph. Each node in the line graph corresponds to an edge in the original graph, with attributes: - `original_edge_id`: ID of the original edge - `original_source`: node ID of the original edge's source - `original_target`: node ID of the original edge's target - `original_weight`: weight of the original edge (only present if it has one) A graph with no edges gives an empty line graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For a graph $G = (V, E)$, the line graph $L(G)$ has one node for each edge of $G$, with two nodes in $L(G)$ adjacent whenever the corresponding edges of $G$ share an endpoint. On directed graphs the sharing must respect direction: edge $(u, v)$ links to $(v, w)$ but not to $(w, v)$. From that definition follow several handy identities. $|V(L(G))| = |E(G)|$ by construction, and for undirected $G$ the edge count is $|E(L(G))| = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_v \deg(v)^2 - |E(G)|$. The line graph of $K_n$ is the triangular graph $T(n)$; the line graph of an $n$-cycle is another $n$-cycle; and the line graph of a star $K_{1,n}$ is the complete graph $K_n$, because all $n$ spokes share the hub. Whitney's theorem (1932) makes the whole construction robust: except for the degenerate case of $K_3$ vs $K_{1,3}$, $L(G) \cong L(H)$ implies $G \cong H$. That property is what makes line graphs useful for edge clustering, edge-community analysis, and modeling transfer points in transportation networks. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The path "A -- B -- C" has two edges, so its line graph has two nodes. They are joined by one edge because both original edges meet at "B": ::: {#2debc40a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) lg = g.line_graph() lg.count_nodes(), lg.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (2, 1) ``` ::: ::: The line graph of a triangle is again a triangle: three edges, each sharing an endpoint with the other two: ::: {#c912917e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) lg = g.line_graph() lg.count_nodes(), lg.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (3, 3) ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph, line-graph edges follow the direction of travel. In the chain "A -> B -> C", edge "A -> B" leads into edge "B -> C", giving one directed line-graph edge (shown here with the `"-"` node labels, which use node IDs): ::: {#91fceb96 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) lg = g.line_graph() lg.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['1-2->2-3'] ``` ::: ::: Each line-graph node records which original edge it came from, including that edge's endpoints and weight, so results computed on the line graph can be mapped back: ::: {#813227dc .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes(["X", "Y", "Z"]) g.add_edges([("X", "Y", 2.0), ("Y", "Z", 3.0)]) lg = g.line_graph() lg.get_node_df().select( "label", "original_edge_id", "original_source", "original_target", "original_weight" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
